script: How I Handled Being the Only Person in a Group Project Who Gave a Single Shit. Long ago, I was a university student majoring in literature, juggling lit classes and a project that felt like a nightmare in a dorm room. The professor was a zany dude who made "Madness in Classic Literature" feel like a rollercoaster. But here's the thing… the assignment landed like a bomb: groups of three, 30‑minute presentation on madness in any era of lit. I paired up with two book‑ish people. One was all about 1800s Scotland; she could talk for hours about that vibe. She convinced us to focus on Lord Byron and some existential, devil‑talking guy. What I didn't know was that she was basically a walking meme about Scotland and my partners were doing nothing. We got a weird nod from the professor after class. He said it was "scarce" and would help find sources. However, when we handed him our plan, he just gave us a half‑hearted smile and a "good luck" shrug. Until that moment, I had no clue how far off they'd go. The material we were supposed to read was a mind‑numbing text about a guy who either hallucinated or had a freak religious experience. It was like the most boring, word‑filled sludge I'd ever read. And that's when everything changed: I realized I was the only one actually reading. My partners didn't even skim the Byron poem. They were like, "No jerks here, we got this." I was left with the full weight of the project. If this didn't work, I'd lose the grade, my reputation, and maybe even my sanity. I dove in and did the entire thing solo, from research to handouts. I memorized every line, like a parrot with a PhD. I made bullet points that looked like a cheat sheet but actually had zero substance. On the day of the presentation, I handed out the worksheets to my partners. They looked relieved, thinking I had a plan. They didn't know I was the only one who knew the damn thing. We stood up, and I started talking about madness in 1800s Scotland, going deep into Byron and the devil‑talking protagonist—whose name I remembered because I'd read it. I kept the flow smooth, while they nodded like they were on a different planet. But here's the thing… my partners were silently, gravely nodding along for the whole 30 minutes. The Q&A began. A classmate asked about the religious aspects. I could have answered but instead gave a long, pregnant pause. I let my partners answer, if they wanted, and I stared at them. What I didn't know was how many people were watching my every move. The silence was louder than any shout. I let those excruciating seconds drag on each time a question came. I stared at my partners, waiting for a slip. And that's when everyone realized I was the only one who actually knew about the 19th‑century Scottish madness. It was petty, I'll admit. I was like, "I am not going to be the student who rats out my teammates, but they can't get off scot‑free." I let them think we were fine until the truth came out. After the presentation, the professor pulled me aside. He said he'd grade us separately. I got an A, and my partners? They stopped talking to me. What did they get? I never found out. And that's where we leave it… a cliffhanger that makes your heart race.
